summary: Updates the Sieve reject extension from RFC 3028 so a message can be refused during delivery instead of by sending a bounce. This helps avoid contributing to floods of bounces after forged-sender spam. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3028 and updates RFC 5228.

plainLanguage.summary:
A Sieve script is the small program that decides what to do with an incoming message. This RFC gives it a way to refuse a message that stops during the delivery connection, so the sending server learns at once that the message was refused.

That matters because the usual way to refuse a message, sending a report to whoever the message claims to come from, can be aimed at an innocent address. The report is then generated by the victim's own mail server and goes to a stranger. Refusing early removes most of that risk.

questions: how to reject mail without sending bounce messages
difference between sieve reject and ereject
how to reject mail without sending a bounce
subtitle: Lets a Sieve mail filter refuse a message during delivery, so no bounce goes to a forged sender.

tldr.problem: A mail filter that refuses a message used to have to send a failure report back to the sender. Spammers forge that sender address, so the report lands on an innocent third party, who then receives automated bounces and angry complaints. This is known as a Joe-job.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lets a Sieve script refuse the message at the SMTP or LMTP level, with a 550 response, so the sending server is told straight away and no report is needed. It also defines a new action, ereject, which always prefers that protocol-level refusal.
tldr.outcome: Refusing early removes most of the chance of a misdirected report. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3028, updates RFC 5228, and asks script generators to use ereject instead of reject wherever possible.

facts.label: Enhanced error code for a refusal

today: RFC 5429 is a Proposed Standard from March 2009. It obsoletes RFC 3028 and updates RFC 5228, the base Sieve specification, and nothing has obsoleted it in turn.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Sieve mail filtering language, as originally defined in RFC 3028, specified that the "reject" action shall discard a message and send a Message Disposition Notification to the envelope sender along with an explanatory message. The Sieve language, as updated in RFC 5228, does not define any "reject" action, hence the purpose of this document.

This document updates the definition of the "reject" action to permit refusal of the message during the SMTP transaction, if possible, and defines a new "ereject" action to require refusal of the message during the SMTP transaction, if possible.

An important goal of the document is to reduce the risk of Sieve scripts being used to perpetrate "Joe-job" spam runs, where the notification of non-delivery is in fact sent to an innocent third party. By rejecting the message at the protocol level, it is less likely that a notification will be needed, and thus less likely that one will be misdirected at an innocent third party.

Implementations are further encouraged to use spam-detection systems to determine the level of risk associated with sending a notification, and the document allows implementations to silently drop the notification if the rejected message is deemed likely to be spam.

In general, a Message Disposition Notification is generated by a mail user agent and can indicate the status of a message with respect to its recipient, while a Delivery Status Notification is generated by a mail transfer agent and can indicate whether a message was received and delivered by the mail system.
sections.plainLanguage: Rejecting a message by mail is risky, because the address the report is sent to is one the sender chose. A spammer can put someone else's address there and turn the victim's mail server into a spam source. Saying no during the delivery connection avoids that entirely.

sections.title: The ereject Action
sections.content:
The usage is ereject <reason: string>. Implementations that implement the action must use the "ereject" capability string.

The action cancels the implicit keep and refuses delivery of a message. The reason string is a UTF-8 string specifying the reason for refusal. How the message is refused depends on the capabilities of the mail component executing the Sieve script. The interpreter must carry out the most preferable action possible and must fall back to lesser actions if a preferred action fails. In order from most to least preferred, it must either refuse message delivery by sending a 5XX response code over SMTP or LMTP, or send a non-delivery report to the envelope sender, unless the envelope sender address is determined to be a forged or otherwise invalid address.

The determination of whether an envelope sender is a forgery may be performed by site-specific and implementation-specific heuristic techniques, such as return-path verification. Implementations should log instances when a non-delivery report is not sent, and the reason for not sending it.

The "ereject" action must not be available in environments that do not support protocol-level rejection, such as a mail user agent, and must be available in all other environments that support the "reject" action.

If a message is arriving over SMTP and has multiple recipients, some of whom have accepted it, the document defines how to reject such a message: the server must accept the message and generate Delivery Status Notifications for all the recipients that are refusing it. This exception does not apply to LMTP, which is able to reject messages on a per-recipient basis, although the LMTP client may then have no choice but to generate a Delivery Status Notification to report the error, which may result in blowback spam.
sections.plainLanguage: The ereject action tells the mail server to say no at the point where the message is being delivered. It prefers that, and falls back to sending a report only when the server cannot do it, and never sends that report to an address it believes is forged.

sections.title: The reject Action
sections.content:
This section updates the definition of the "reject" action in Section 4.1 of RFC 3028 and is an optional extension to RFC 5228. The usage is reject <reason: string>, and implementations that implement it must use the "reject" capability string.

The action cancels the implicit keep and refuses delivery of a message. Unlike "ereject", this action always favours preserving the exact text of the refusal reason. Typically, it refuses delivery by sending back a Message Disposition Notification to the sender. However, implementations may refuse delivery over SMTP or LMTP if and only if the reason string consists only of US-ASCII characters, or contains non-US-ASCII and both the client and server support and negotiate an SMTP or LMTP extension for sending UTF-8 responses; and if LMTP is used, or SMTP is used and the message has a single recipient, or SMTP is used with multiple recipients and all of them refused message delivery.

When the action does send a notification, it resends the received message to the envelope sender specified by the MAIL FROM or Return-Path address, wrapping it in a "reject" form and explaining that it was rejected by the recipient. A reject message must take the form of a failure Message Disposition Notification. The human-readable portion contains the message describing the error, and should contain additional text alerting the apparent original sender that mail was refused by an email filter. The disposition field must be "deleted" and must have the "MDN-sent-automatically" and "automatic-action" modes set.

Implementations may use the techniques of the "ereject" section to decide whether a non-delivery report should not be sent to a forged sender, and should log instances when a report is not sent and the reason.
sections.plainLanguage: The reject action is the older behaviour with one addition: it may also refuse the message during delivery, but only when the reason text can be sent exactly. Otherwise it sends the message back to the sender with a note explaining that it was refused.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Sieve Actions
sections.content:
Both "reject" and "ereject" cancel the implicit keep. Implementations must prohibit the execution of more than one "reject" in a Sieve script, and "reject" must be incompatible with the "vacation" action. It is not recommended that implementations permit the use of "reject" with actions that cause mail delivery, such as "keep", "fileinto" and "redirect".

Making "reject" compatible with actions that cause mail delivery violates the RFC 5321 principle that a message is either delivered or bounced back to the sender, because bouncing a message back and delivering it will make the sender believe that the message was not delivered. The RFC notes, however, that there are existing laws requiring certain organizations to archive all received messages, even rejected ones, and that saving copies of rejected messages for later analysis can be useful.

Any action that would modify the message body will not have an effect on the body of a message refused with an SMTP response code, and must not have any effect on the content of generated Delivery Status Notifications or Message Disposition Notifications.

On upgrading: implementations must not silently upgrade "reject" actions to "ereject" actions in a Sieve script, because this might lead to unpleasant changes of behaviour not expected by the script owner. User interfaces that present a generic rejection option may switch from generating "reject" to "ereject" actions, so long as doing so does not create a confusing change for the script owner. Script generators should ensure that a rejection action executed as a result of an anti-spam or anti-virus test uses the "ereject" action, as it is more suitable for such rejections, and may automatically upgrade scripts that previously used "reject" for that purpose, provided the target environment can support it.
sections.plainLanguage: A script may refuse a message only once, and it must not both refuse a message and let it through, because the sender would be told the message was not delivered when it was. Tools that write Sieve scripts should use the new action for spam rejections, but must not quietly rewrite an existing script.

sections.title: Protocol-Level Refusal in Detail
sections.content:
Sieve implementations that are able to reject messages at the SMTP or LMTP level must do so and should use the 550 response code. If the reason string consists of multiple lines separated by CRLF, the reason text must be returned as a multiline SMTP or LMTP response, and no line may exceed the SMTP limit on maximal line length; the server may insert CRLFs to make the response conform.

If the SMTP or LMTP server supports RFC 2034, it must prepend an appropriate Enhanced Error Code to the reason text. Enhanced Error Code 5.7.1, or the more generic 5.7.0, are recommended.

SMTP does not allow non-US-ASCII characters in the response text. If non-US-ASCII characters appear in the reason string, they can be sent at the protocol level only if the client and the server use an SMTP extension that allows non-US-ASCII reply text. In the absence of such an extension, the Sieve engine must replace the reason string being sent at the protocol level with an implementation-defined US-ASCII-only string. Users who do not like this behaviour should consider the "reject" action, which always preserves the exact reason text.

If a Sieve implementation that supports "ereject" does not wish to disclose immediately the reason for rejection, for example that it detected spam, it may delay sending the 550 error code by sending a 4XX error code on the first attempt to receive the message.
sections.plainLanguage: Refusing over the protocol means answering the sending server with an error code, normally 550, and putting the reason text in that answer. If the reason contains characters the protocol cannot carry, the engine has to substitute something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The introduction discusses why rejecting messages before delivery is better than accepting and bouncing them.

The details of the techniques that can be used to decide when to silently drop a non-delivery report are outside the scope of the document, but the explicit permission it gives to take such action may enable denial-of-service situations. Techniques such as spam-checking and return-path verification can and do have false positives, so care should be exercised to prevent the loss of legitimate messages by failing to notify the sender of non-delivery.

Security issues associated with email auto-responders are discussed in the security considerations of RFC 3834, and the document is not believed to introduce any additional security considerations in that general area. The "ereject" extension does not raise any other security considerations beyond those already present in the base Sieve specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Not sending a report to a suspected forged address is useful, but the checks that spot a forged address sometimes get it wrong. The RFC warns that this permission could be used to make a mail server refuse to report a legitimate refusal, so the checks need care.
